Industry observers note that the energy cost of a ϕ displacement is only due to U ∝ ħΩ, but the cost of a Z displacement also includes an interaction-energy penalty, ∝ μs. The ratio of these costs gives the ratio of the oscillation amplitudes:.

and their product gives the plasma-oscillation frequency.

In the non-interacting (Rabi) limit AZ = AY and ωp = Ω, and in the Josephson regime AZ ≪ AY, which is essential for the implementation of the sine-Gordon model, and \(\hbar {\omega }_{{\rm{p}}}\approx \sqrt{2\hbar \varOmega {\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}}\gg \hbar \varOmega \) is the mass gap m*c2 in equation (1).

Our measurements (Fig. 3c) agree with the predictions of equations (3) and (4) over three orders of magnitude in μs/(ħΩ). Crucially, we observe coherent oscillations deep in the Josephson regime, up to μs/(ħΩ) ≈ 102.

Next, we turn to the finite-momentum (k > 0) spin excitations (Fig. 4). By modulating Ω at frequency ωm, we parametrically excite finite-k spin modes with frequency ωs(k) = ωm/2 (Fig. 4a). It is noted that the coupling of this parametric drive to the total-density modes is much weaker. Figure 4b indicates example images with and without parametric modulation. We measure n−i(x, y), which reveals the ϕ excitations. For every ωm, we observe ϕ modulations with a well-defined spatial frequency k, and thus map out the spin dispersion relation, shown in Fig. 4c for different m* values.

a, Experimental protocol. We parametrically excite the system by modulating Ω at frequency ωm. The injected energy, in quanta of ħωm, is converted to pairs of spatial excitations with opposite momenta, each carrying energy ħωm/2. b, Example measurements. Top: after the parametric modulation, images of n−i show fluctuations with a characteristic ωm-dependent length scale. Scale bar, 20 μm. Bottom: normalizing the spatial power spectrum of the fluctuations observed with modulation to that without modulation, we reveal the dominant k excited at each ωm, which gives ωs(k) = ωm/2. Each data point is based on five independent experimental runs; the symbols show the mean values and the error bars denote the s.e.m. The solid lines show Gaussian fits. c, Dispersion relations for different field masses m*, tuned by varying the value of Ω (around which we modulate); here we also include k = 0 plasma-oscillation measurements. The solid lines show theoretical predictions from equation (5). The dashed lines indicate the inverse magnetic healing lengths \(1/{\xi }_{{\rm{M}}}=\sqrt{2m\varOmega /\hbar }\); in our system, ξM corresponds to the reduced Compton wavelength ħ/(m*c). The dotted line shows the inverse spin healing length, \(1/{\xi }_{{\rm{s}}}=\sqrt{2m{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}/{\hbar }^{2}}\), which sets the low-k range where the dispersion is approximately relativistic (see text). The error bars in k denote the Gaussian widths of the spectra such as shown in b. For these measurements Z0 = 0.31.

The measured dispersion is in good agreement with the theoretical prediction5,19 (see also Methods).

Sources indicate that where ϵk = ħ2k2/(2m). For k ≲ 1/ξs ≈ 2.6 μm−1, where \({\xi }_{{\rm{s}}}=\sqrt{{\hbar }^{2}/(2m{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}})}\) is the spin healing length, this prediction is close to the massive relativistic dispersion relation.

Sources indicate that where we now use the more general expressions for \(c\approx \sqrt{(\hbar \varOmega +{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}})/m}\) and \({m}^{\ast }\approx m\sqrt{\hbar \varOmega (\hbar \varOmega +2{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}})/{(\hbar \varOmega +{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}})}^{2}}\), which are valid for any μs/(ħΩ); see Extended Data Fig. 1 for a comparison between equations (5) and (6).

For Ω = 0, the dispersion is gapless, while a non-zero Ω opens up a gap at k = 0 (see also ref. 38). For a massive relativistic field, the transition from the low-energy quadratic dispersion to the higher-energy linear dispersion is set by the reduced Compton wavelength ƛ = ħ/(m*c), which here corresponds to the magnetic (Rabi) healing length \({\xi }_{{\rm{M}}}=\sqrt{\hbar /(2m\varOmega )}\). Our ability to tune \({\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}/(\hbar \varOmega )={({\xi }_{{\rm{M}}}/{\xi }_{{\rm{s}}})}^{2}\gg 1\) gives us a k range where the relativistic nature of the massive dispersion is crucial.

We now turn to exploring the non-perturbative sine-Gordon dynamics, by initializing the system at a large global phase displacement ϕ0 (Fig. 5a).

a, We study the dynamics following a large initial phase displacement ϕ0. For ∣ϕ0∣ < π, the plasma-oscillation period is ϕ0-dependent owing to the concavity of U(ϕ). For ϕ0 = π, different regions of the system may eventually settle to different potential minima, which results in domain walls across which ϕ winds by 2π. b, Large-amplitude oscillations. Left: for different ϕ0, the system takes different time, τ, to return to ϕ = 0. Solid lines show sinusoidal fits; for large ϕ0, the oscillation is visibly anharmonic. Each data point is based on five independent experimental runs, and the error bars show the s.e.m. Right: τ/τ0 versus ϕ0; here τ0 = π/(2ωp) is the ϕ0-independent perturbative result. The solid line is the prediction based on the pendulum model. The errors in τ correspond to half of the spacing between the sampled t values. Here, Z0 = 0.31, Ω/(2π) = 74 Hz and μs/(ħΩ) ≈ 11. c,d, Domain walls. The system is prepared at ϕ ≈ π at t = 0, and allowed to relax for 10 ms, corresponding to approximately 7τ0; here Z0 = 0.53, Ω/(2π) = 22 Hz and μs/(ħΩ) ≈ 39. Scale bar, 20 μm. In c, we show examples of domain walls seen in n+ and n− images, where they appear as, respectively, low- and high-density lines; each image shows an independent realization. In d, we show phase maps that reveal the 2π phase winding at domain walls. We interfere the two spin states using a pair of Raman–Bragg laser beams with wavevectors q1,2, and the imaged density distribution, nRB, shows modulations \(\propto \cos ({\bf{q}}\cdot {\bf{r}}+\phi )\), where q = q1 − q2 and r = (x, y). From such fringe patterns we reconstruct the phase maps shown in the bottom panels (see text for details).

According to recent reports, for ∣ϕ0∣ < π, we observe the anharmonic nature of the sine-Gordon potential, \(U(\phi )\propto -\cos (\phi )\), by measuring the time, τ, it takes the system to return from ϕ0 to ϕ = 0 (Fig. 5b). Here, we extract \(\phi =\arctan (Y/X)\), where Y and X are the separately measured projections of the global Bloch vector. In the perturbative regime, U(ϕ) is approximately harmonic and τ ≈ π/(2ωp) is independent of ϕ0. However, as ϕ0 → π, the concavity of U becomes increasingly relevant and τ grows, in analogy with a mechanical pendulum with a large initial angular displacement (solid line in Fig. 5b, right). At longer times these oscillations damp out, and this damping is accompanied by an emergence of spatial structures corresponding to k > 0 excitations (Extended Data Fig. 2).

For ϕ0 = π, different regions of the system may settle into different potential minima, leading to the formation of domain walls across which ϕ rapidly winds by 2π. We observe such walls in most experimental realizations, with their spatial patterns varying randomly shot to shot (Fig. 5c,d).

It has been revealed that in the images of n+ and n− (Fig. 5c), the walls appear as lines of low and high density, respectively. Here we show images from different experimental realizations, but note that if we image both n+ and n− in the same experimental run, we see that they are complementary (Extended Data Fig. 3).

Industry observers note that in Fig. 5d, we explicitly demonstrate the 2π phase winding across the domain walls. Here, just before imaging the \(|\uparrow \rangle \) component, we perform a fast (approximately 6 μs) π/2 spin rotation using a resonant two-photon Raman–Bragg coupling (see cartoon) instead of a radio-frequency field. Compared with the radio-frequency field that has a spatially uniform phase across the cloud, the Raman–Bragg coupling leads to a complex Ω with a spatially varying phase q ⋅ r; here r = (x, y) and q = q1 − q2, where q1,2 are the wavevectors of the two laser beams. In the Bloch-sphere picture, the Raman–Bragg Rabi vector always lies in the equatorial plane, but its orientation varies along the direction defined by q. Consequently, the imaged density nRB(x, y) reveals modulations \(\propto \cos ({\bf{q}}\cdot {\bf{r}}+\phi )\). For a spatially uniform ϕ, this is a pattern of straight parallel fringes with period 2π/q ≈ 2.51 μm, whereas spatial variations of ϕ(x, y) lead to fringe deformations. In particular, a domain wall perpendicular to q changes the fringe spacing, whereas a wall parallel to q shifts the fringe phase by 2π. In Fig. 5d, we show both  the straight fringes observed at t = 0 ms and two examples of domain walls observed after 10 ms of relaxation; the bottom panels show the reconstructed phase maps (see Extended Data Fig. 4 for more details).

According to recent reports, the characteristic width, w, of an equilibrium domain wall is set by the competition between the potential energy per unit length, ∝ ħΩ ⋅ nw, and the corresponding kinetic energy, ∝ ħ2/(2mw2) ⋅ nw. Similarly to the oscillator length in a quantum harmonic oscillator, this competition gives w = ƛ = \({\xi }_{{\rm{M}}}=\sqrt{\hbar /(2m\varOmega )}\).

In Fig. 6a, we extract the domain-wall widths from both the n± images and the phase maps. In all cases, one-dimensional cuts perpendicular to the walls are fitted well by the theoretically predicted10 forms n±(z) = n0 ± n1sech2(z/w) and ϕ(z) = 4arctan[exp(z/w)]; here, z is the coordinate perpendicular to a wall centred at z = 0, and n0, n1 and w are fit parameters. The extracted values of w have a wide distribution (see histograms), probably because our domain walls are excited, but the three mean values are (within one standard deviation) consistent with each other and with the theoretically predicted w, indicated on the histograms by the dashed lines; it is noted that here we include an 8% correction to the predicted w due to our non-zero Z0 (Methods).

Industry observers note that a, For the experimental protocol as in Fig. 5, we extract the wall widths, w, from n+ and n− images, such as shown in Fig. 5c, and the phase maps, such as shown in Fig. 5d. We fit cuts perpendicular to the walls to the theoretically expected profiles (solid lines, see text). The histograms show width distributions based on >100 experimental images, and the dashed lines indicate the theoretically predicted w. b, The effect of changing Ω on the domain-wall width. Here the experimental protocol is the same, except that for the last 2 ms of relaxation we jump Ω/(2π) from 22 Hz to either 10 Hz or 45 Hz. The representative n+ images show an increase of the wall widths in the former case and decrease in the latter. Scale bar, 20 μm. The summary of the extracted mean widths is consistent with the expected trend \(w\propto 1/\sqrt{\varOmega }\). The dashed line highlights the theoretically predicted w, including an 8% correction due to our non-zero Z0 (Methods). The solid line shows the same trend with systematically 15% lower values. The error bars show the standard deviations of the w distributions. The different symbols corresponding to the same Ω are slightly offset horizontally for clarity.

Finally, in Fig. 6b, we show that the characteristic wall width responds to changes in Ω. Here we initiate the system dynamics as in Fig. 5c, but quench Ω either down or up for the last 2 ms of relaxation. In the representative n+ images, one can see the systematic change in the wall widths, and the widths extracted as in Fig. 6a are consistent with the expected trend \(w\propto 1/\sqrt{\varOmega }\).

Recent findings suggest that to conclude, we have established a versatile analogue simulator for self-interacting relativistic quantum fields with a tunable mass in 2 + 1 dimensions, and observed non-perturbative phenomena that point the way to many future studies. The damping of the global ϕ oscillations, accompanied by an emergence of spatial structures (k > 0 excitations), is expected to be analogous to cosmological preheating and reheating11,12. The π phase jump that places the field at the top of the sine-Gordon potential initiates dynamics associated with a quench through a discrete symmetry-breaking phase transition (with the energy minima changing from ϕ = π to ϕ = 0 and 2π). Generalizing the π phase jump to a ramp of Ω from a positive to a negative value, one can study the associated Kibble–Zurek mechanism50, linked to the formation of topological defects such as cosmic strings and domain walls13,14. Studies of domain-wall networks could provide insights into cosmological dark-matter production in axion scenarios51,52 and gravitational-wave signals in a broad family of particle-physics models53. In this context, a particularly interesting possibility is to use vector light shifts to deterministically imprint specific initial domain-wall configurations and study their subsequent dynamics, including their relaxation and decay54,55. Finally, using Floquet engineering to stabilize the system at ϕ = π would enable studies of false-vacuum decay15,16,41,42 in a relativistic, cosmologically relevant setting17,18,19.

It has been revealed that our experiments were performed in a uniform two-dimensional optical box trap formed by repulsive 532-nm light. The two-dimensional confinement was provided by an accordion lattice with trapping frequency ωz/(2π) ≈ 1 kHz, generated holographically56 with a digital micro-mirror device. The in-plane confinement was provided by a square box directly projected from another digital micro-mirror device through a high-resolution microscope (numerical aperture 0.7). The box size was approximately 50 μm × 50 μm for Fig. 1c, and 30 μm × 30 μm for the rest of the experiments.

The radio-frequency field that couples the two hyperfine states was derived from a vector signal generator (Keysight N5172B). Using in-phase and quadrature modulation, we independently and simultaneously controlled the amplitude, phase and frequency of the radio-frequency field; to prevent carrier feed-through from contaminating the signal, we used a 200-kHz baseband offset. This allowed us to dynamically attenuate the radio-frequency power by >60 dB, and realize Ω/(2π) ≲ 10Hz while retaining the ability to perform fast π/2 rotation at Ω/(2π) > 10kHz. The calibration error for Ω was ≲1% (standard deviation).

To stabilize the magnetic field B, we first regulated the current through our coils using a feedback loop with a bandwidth >1 kHz and then cancelled the residual 50-Hz mains oscillations using feedforward. This cancelled most of the high-frequency noise from the power supply. To counter slow thermal drifts, we periodically (approximately once per minute) calibrated the field using partial Landau–Zener transfers. On the basis of Zerr from the calibration data, we estimated the residual field variations to be about 150 μG (root mean square).

Sources indicate that the two-dimensional interaction parameters are given by \({g}_{\sigma {\sigma }^{{\prime} }}=\)\(({\hbar }^{2}/m)\sqrt{8{\rm{\pi }}}\,{a}_{\sigma {\sigma }^{{\prime} }}/{{\ell }}_{z}\), where \({a}_{\sigma {\sigma }^{{\prime} }}\) are the s-wave scattering lengths, which we calculate using coupled-channel calculations57,58, and \({{\ell }}_{z}=\sqrt{\hbar /(m{\omega }_{z})}\) (ref. 47).

where \({g}_{{\rm{d}}}=({g}_{\uparrow \uparrow }{g}_{\downarrow \downarrow }-{g}_{\uparrow \downarrow }^{2})/({g}_{\uparrow \uparrow }+{g}_{\downarrow \downarrow }-2{g}_{\uparrow \downarrow })\), κ = (g↑↑ + g↓↓ − 2g↑↓)/4, and Z0 = − Δ/κ, with Δ = (g↑↑ − g↓↓)/4.

The two relevant interaction-energy scales are then μd = gdn for the density degrees of freedom (which for Z = Z0 reduces to the standard density chemical potential) and μs = κn for the spin degrees of freedom.

Sources indicate that for Ω ≫ μs/ħ and δ = 0, the plasma frequencies for oscillations near ϕ = 0 and ϕ = π are \({\omega }_{{\rm{p}},0}=\sqrt{\varOmega (\varOmega +2{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}/\hbar )}\) and \({\omega }_{{\rm{p}},{\rm{\pi }}}=\sqrt{\varOmega (\varOmega -2{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}/\hbar )}\). By measuring ωp,0 − ωp,π ≈ 2μs/ħ, we calibrate μs and hence n. We summarize the interaction parameters relevant for our experiments in Extended Data Table 1.

Here trigonometric corrections owing to non-zero Z0 are incorporated through the factor \(\alpha =(1-{Z}_{0}^{2})\) and the scaled variables \({\varOmega }^{{\prime} }=\varOmega /\sqrt{\alpha }\), \({\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}^{{\prime} }=\alpha {\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}\) and \(\delta {Z}^{{\prime} }=\delta Z/\alpha \). From equation (9), we can derive various quantities such as the spin dispersion relation.

and the aspect ratios for the plasma oscillations.

In the main text we give the simpler and more intuitive approximate equations that assume Z0 = 0. For all expressions in the main text other than equations (2) and (3), for which the exact forms can be obtained from equations (9) and (11), the corrections due to non-zero Z0 can be incorporated by simply replacing Ω by Ω′ and μs by \({\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}^{{\prime} }\). For our experiments, these corrections are usually negligible (compared with the statistical errors), as we illustrate in Fig. 3c by plotting both the predictions that take into account the Z0 corrections (dotted lines) and the approximate predictions that assume Z0 = 0 (solid lines). For Figs. 4 and 5, the corrections are similarly negligible and for simplicity we ignore them, using only the simpler theory given in the main text. The only perceptible correction, which we do include when comparing the data with theory, is in Fig. 6, where, for Z0 = 0.53, the expected wall width \(w=\sqrt{\hbar /(2m{\varOmega }^{{\prime} })}\) is approximately 8% smaller than \(\sqrt{\hbar /(2m\varOmega )}\).

In Extended Data Fig. 1, we also examine the range of k values for which the dispersion of our spin modes, ωs(k) in equation (5), mimics well the relativistic dispersion ωr(k) in equation (6). As long as k < 1/ξs, the difference between ωs and ωr is ≲20% even for Ω = 0, and it reduces with increasing Ω.

Industry observers note that most importantly, the domain walls we observe in Figs. 5 and 6 are deep in the long-wavelength, relativistic regime. For these walls, the relevant k modes are k ≲ 1/w, and even for our largest Ω in Fig. 6, 1/w is still smaller than the smallest 1/ξM (purple dashed line) shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. In this k range, ωs(k) and ωr(k) are essentially identical.

Industry observers note that in Extended Data Fig. 2, we illustrate how the large-amplitude plasma oscillations, such as shown in Fig. 5b, damp at long times. This damping is accompanied by emergence of spatial structures corresponding to a transfer of energy from k = 0 to higher-k modes; qualitatively, this is what is expected in models of cosmological preheating and reheating11,12.

In Extended Data Fig. 3, we create domain walls as in Fig. 5c, and take consecutive images of n+ and n− in the same experimental run, which demonstrates that the two density distributions are complementary.

In a recent development, from our nRB(x, y) images, we extract ϕtot = q ⋅ r + ϕ using a convolutional neural network59, trained on synthetic data that mimic the experimental images. The network generates quadrature maps I(x, y) and Q(x, y) that approximate, respectively, \(\cos [{\phi }_{{\rm{tot}}}(x,y)]\) and \(\sin [{\phi }_{{\rm{tot}}}(x,y)]\), and we extract ϕtot(x, y) as the phase of I(x, y) + iQ(x, y).

In Extended Data Fig. 4, we illustrate the fidelity of this extraction for two examples shown in Fig. 5d and two additional ones from the same dataset. Left to right, we show: (1) the nRB images, (2) the reconstructed \([1+\cos ({\phi }_{{\rm{tot}}})]/2\), which is essentially the de-noised version of the fringes seen in nRB, (3) the contours tracing the maxima of the reconstructed fringes, (4) the overlaying of these contours on the original images, and (5) the extracted ϕ(x, y).

Recent findings suggest that we obtain ϕ(x, y) from ϕtot(x, y) by subtracting the independently calibrated carrier phase q ⋅ r, but note that, because the relative phase between the Raman–Bragg beams and the radio-frequency coupling is random, our measurement determines ϕ(x, y) only up to a global offset. We fix this offset such that ⟨eiϕ⟩ is real and negative for t = 0 ms (as ϕ is jumped to π), and real and positive for t = 10 ms (appropriate for relaxation to ϕ = 0 (mod 2π), as observed in the n± images).

Recent findings suggest that we illustrate our phase-extraction process and its fidelity for two examples from Fig. 5d and two additional ones. We extract ϕtot = q ⋅ r + ϕ from the nRB images using a convolutional neural network59 trained on synthetic data. Here we show the reconstructed fringe pattern \([1+\cos ({\phi }_{{\rm{tot}}})]/2\), the contours tracing the reconstructed-fringe maxima, and the overlays of these contours on the original experimental images. To obtain ϕ(x, y), we subtract from ϕtot the independently calibrated carrier phase q ⋅ r. This determines ϕ only up to a global offset, because the relative phase between the Raman–Bragg beams and the radio-frequency coupling is random from shot to shot. For the data in Fig. 5d, we fix this offset by centering the ϕ-distribution on π for t = 0 ms, and on 0 for t = 10 ms. The fringe period 2π/q is 2.51 ± 0.04 μm, with the error originating from Fourier broadening. Scale bar, 20 μm.
